intro: Friedman was as formidable on a stage or a talk show as in print. He debated with a smile, took every question from a hostile audience, and could reduce a chapter of monetary theory to a sentence. These are the speeches, lectures and interviews that mattered most, with a line from each.

items.title: The Wabash lectures
items.quote: The free man will ask neither what his country can do for him nor what he can do for his country.
items.context: A series of lectures for the Volker Fund, transcribed by Rose, that became Capitalism and Freedom. The line, answering Kennedy's inaugural five years before it was delivered as such, opens the book's introduction.

items.title: Inflation: Causes and Consequences
items.quote: Inflation is always and everywhere a monetary phenomenon in the sense that it is and can be produced only by a more rapid increase in the quantity of money than in output.
items.context: Lectures given in India during a visit to advise on economic policy. The sentence became the most quoted summary of monetarism.
items.source: Inflation: Causes and Consequences (Asia Publishing House, 1963)

items.title: The Role of Monetary Policy
items.venue: American Economic Association presidential address, Washington, D.C.
items.quote: There is always a temporary trade-off between inflation and unemployment; there is no permanent trade-off.
items.context: The address that introduced the natural rate of unemployment and predicted the stagflation of the following decade. Published in the American Economic Review in March 1968.

items.title: Testimony to the Gates Commission on the draft
items.venue: President's Commission on an All-Volunteer Armed Force, Washington, D.C.
items.quote: Would you rather command an army of slaves?
items.context: Friedman's reply when General William Westmoreland said he did not want to command an army of mercenaries. Westmoreland, he recalled, never used the word mercenary again. The commission recommended a volunteer force; the draft ended in 1973.

items.title: Lecture in Santiago
items.quote: The shock treatment is the only way to end inflation. The gradual approach merely prolongs the agony.
items.context: A public lecture on inflation during the six-day visit that led to protests for years afterwards. Friedman defended his visit as advice, not endorsement, and said he had given the same advice in Yugoslavia and China.
items.source: Two Lucky People (1998), ch. 24 and appendix

items.title: Nobel banquet speech
items.quote: My science is a late-comer, having achieved full recognition only in 1969.
items.context: A short, modest speech noting that the economics prize was not one of Alfred Nobel's original five, and reflecting on what a scientist owes to the public's incomplete understanding of his work.

items.title: Nobel lecture: Inflation and Unemployment
items.quote: A positive relation between inflation and unemployment may be the rule rather than the exception in periods of high and variable inflation.
items.context: The lecture extends the natural-rate hypothesis to explain the coexistence of inflation and unemployment that Keynesian models could not accommodate.
items.source: Nobel Foundation; Journal of Political Economy 85 (1977)

items.title: On Donahue: the greed question
items.quote: Is there some society you know that doesn't run on greed? The world runs on individuals pursuing their separate interests.
items.context: Asked whether he ever had doubts about capitalism when he saw greed around him, Friedman asked where the host had found a society that ran on anything else. The two-minute exchange has been watched tens of millions of times.
items.source: Donahue, 1979; clip circulated by the Free To Choose Network

items.title: Free to Choose, episode 1: The Power of the Market
items.quote: Look at this lead pencil. There's not a single person in the world who could make this pencil.
items.context: Standing in a market and holding up a pencil, Friedman restates Leonard Read's I, Pencil to show how prices coordinate the work of thousands of strangers who do not know one another. The opening episode of the ten-part series.

items.title: Free to Choose, episode 2: The Tyranny of Control
items.quote: The record of history is absolutely crystal clear, that there is no alternative way so far discovered of improving the lot of the ordinary people that can hold a candle to the productive activities that are unleashed by the free enterprise system.
items.context: From the studio debate that followed the film, in answer to a question about the poor. Clips of this exchange are among the most shared of his career.

items.title: Free to Choose, episode 5: Created Equal
items.quote: A society that puts equality before freedom will get neither. A society that puts freedom before equality will get a high degree of both.
items.context: The episode distinguishes equality before God, equality of opportunity and equality of outcome, and argues that only the first two are compatible with liberty.

items.title: Tyranny of the Status Quo
items.quote: Nothing is so permanent as a temporary government program.
items.context: The three-part series with Rose on why reform has only a brief window before the beneficiaries of the status quo organise to defend it.

items.title: Presidential Medal of Freedom
items.quote: He has used a brilliant mind to advance a moral vision: the vision of a society where men and women are free, free to choose, but where government is not as free to override their decisions.
items.context: President Reagan's citation at the ceremony. Friedman received the National Medal of Science the same year.
items.source: Reagan Presidential Library, remarks of 17 October 1988

items.title: Why Drugs Should Be Legalized
items.quote: The role of the government is to protect the drug cartel. That's literally true.
items.context: An interview with Randy Paige in which Friedman argued that prohibition sustains the cartels' profits, corrupts the police and fills prisons without reducing use.

items.title: Ninetieth birthday conference
items.quote: Regarding the Great Depression, you're right. We did it. We're very sorry. But thanks to you, we won't do it again.
items.context: Federal Reserve governor Ben Bernanke, closing his tribute, conceded the central argument of the Monetary History on behalf of the institution it indicted. Six years later Bernanke, as chairman, acted on that lesson.
items.source: Ben S. Bernanke, remarks at the Conference to Honor Milton Friedman, 8 November 2002

items.title: Interview with Charlie Rose
items.quote: The most important single central fact about a free market is that no exchange takes place unless both parties benefit.
items.context: A full hour at ninety-three, the last long television interview, ranging over his life, the Fed, the euro, Iraq, school choice and drugs.

items.title: Why Money Matters
items.quote: The Fed has only one instrument: the quantity of money.
items.context: Not a speech but a last word: his final article, printed the day after his death, restating the argument of sixty years.
